primary_sources: Harry R. Hopps, "Destroy This Mad Brute" poster, 1917

stimulus.text: The poster shows a huge gorilla wearing a German spiked helmet marked "MILITARISM." The gorilla holds a bloody club marked "KULTUR" in one hand and carries a woman in the other arm. It steps onto ground marked "AMERICA." Large lettering reads: "DESTROY THIS MAD BRUTE / ENLIST / U.S. ARMY." The poster was drawn by Harry R. Hopps in 1917.
stimulus.source_note: Poster by Harry R. Hopps, 1917, public domain (Library of Congress).

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Harry R. Hopps poster, 1917, public domain

rationales.A: American posters in World War II did not picture Japanese soldiers as honorable. They pictured them as a threat.
rationales.B: The poster attacks its enemy. It does not praise an ally.
rationales.C: In both wars, posters turned the enemy into a monster threatening American homes, so that fear would build support for fighting.
rationales.D: The poster attacks its enemy. It does not praise an ally.
rationales.general:
1. Name the poster's move: turn the enemy into a beast threatening America.
2. Ask which later poster used the same move. World War II posters did the same with Japan.
3. Rule out the options that praise an ally or soften the enemy.
Remember: compare posters by the move they make, not just by the war they belong to.
